title: How Cicadas Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain periodic cicadas, focusing on the 17-year and 13-year broods emerging along the US Eastern seaboard in 2013. They cover appearance and anatomy (red eyes, wings, ocelli, stylets, labium), the loud mating calls and how tymbals produce them, mating and egg-laying, the long underground nymph stage, predator satiation as a survival strategy, temperature-triggered synchronized emergence, a formula for predicting emergence dates, their harmlessness to people, and eating cicadas. They promote a Science Channel special, Cicada Invasion 2013. The episode ends with listener mail about scopolamine ("Devil's breath") attacks in Bogota, Colombia, linked to an earlier truth serum episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and cicada introduction
segments.summary: The hosts joke around, settle on the pronunciation 'cicada', and introduce periodic cicadas as the species making news on the Eastern seaboard, pointing listeners to magicicada.org for a map.

segments.title: Science Channel Cicada Invasion 2013 promotion
segments.summary: The hosts promote the Science Channel special Cicada Invasion 2013 airing Sunday, May 20, and their segments with Professor Mike Raupp.

segments.title: Brood timing and the 17-year and 13-year broods
segments.summary: Periodical broods emerge every 13 or 17 years, native only to North America. The 17-year brood is the one emerging on the Eastern seaboard, with billions of insects synchronized, and an estimated density described by Raupp.

segments.title: Cicada appearance and physical features
segments.summary: Adults have black bodies with orange-veined wings and red eyes, with rare blue or silver-eyed variants. They are in the order Hemiptera, have two pairs of wings that they fly poorly with, three pairs of clumsy legs, compound and ocelli eyes, antennae, and a beak-like labium with stylets used for sucking plant sap.

segments.title: Cicada mating songs and loudness
segments.summary: Only males sing, to attract females and scare off birds. The calls reach around 94 decibels, with reports up to 120, and the hosts compare the volume to lawnmowers and rock concerts. Cicadas are closer to aphids than crickets and sing with tymbals, not vocal cords or leg rubbing. They have a protective mechanism that closes their ears while calling.

segments.title: Mating, egg-laying, and nymph life underground
segments.summary: After mating, females cut notches in twigs and lay up to six eggs per session with an ovipositor. Nymphs drop to the ground and burrow, spending about 17 years underground, then emerge for about two to six weeks as adults after molting. Predator satiation and fungal and beetle-larva predators are discussed.

segments.title: Synchronized emergence and temperature cues
segments.summary: Emergence is thought to be triggered by ground temperature, with activity beginning around when soil averages reach about 64 degrees Fahrenheit, and emergence moves north from Georgia through the Carolinas, Virginia, DC, and up to New York. A formula using April temperature predicts local emergence dates.

segments.title: Cicadas as harmless insects and eating them
segments.summary: Cicadas do not bite or sting, carry disease, or kill trees, and males buzz defensively if held. The hosts discuss cicada recipes, cicada cookies, and citizen science projects on cicadas.

segments.title: Listener mail on scopolamine in Colombia
segments.summary: Listener Calaroi Zervos, who lived in Colombia for twelve years, writes about scopolamine attacks in Bogota, where petty thieves dust paper with the drug and hand it to victims, who are then robbed. He corrects the earlier idea that drug traffickers use it, and thanks the hosts for their truth serum episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information and website details and close the episode, with a Netflix sponsor read.
